name: complete-mediation
intent: Route every access to a protected object through a single decision point that re-checks authority at the point of use, so that no later access — on any path, including retry, batch, recovery and maintenance paths — can rely on an earlier check.
problem: Authority is verified where access is first obtained (login, connection setup, first call) and every later path to the object then trusts that context: internal callers, cached handles, background jobs, admin and recovery code reach the object unchecked, and a revocation does not take effect because the earlier decision is remembered. Between checking an access right and performing the access there is also a window in which the checked facts can change.
context: Any system in which a security-relevant resource is reachable through more than one code path: a kernel or runtime mediating syscalls, a server mediating requests through middleware, a guarded subsystem mediating operations on a protected object, or a capability wrapper mediating access to references exchanged through an interface. It applies wherever authority can change while references are still held, and it presupposes an identity on every path, a policy source and an audit sink.
benefits: Completeness becomes checkable: every access attempt passes one place, so the reachable paths can be enumerated, reviewed and tested instead of being inferred from scattered guards.
Revocation and policy changes take effect on the next access, because decisions are made at the point of use rather than inherited from a remembered result.
Time-of-check/time-of-use gaps close where the check and the access are one operation (an open with resolve constraints, row-level policy inside the query, a check inside the guarded method).
Policy lives in one place, so the protected object needs neither ad-hoc guards nor knowledge of who may use it.
Every decision — granted or denied — passes a single point where it can be logged, metered and alarmed on, which is what makes an audit trail trustworthy.
New callers inherit mediation automatically instead of having to remember the guard, which removes the most common way an authorization hole appears.
tradeoffs: A decision on every access costs latency and throughput, and the principle's own literature warns that remembering results for performance reopens the hole: if authority can change, every cached decision needs a bounded lifetime and explicit invalidation on revocation.

The mediator lies on every path, so it is a single point of failure, a throughput bottleneck and the hot spot for every policy change; it stays reviewable only if it is kept small (economy of mechanism) and if policy is separated from enforcement.
Completeness requires an identity on every path: batch, recovery, maintenance and administrative paths that carry no principal must be given one, or the mediation degenerates into a rubber stamp.

Confinement: as soon as the mediator hands out a raw reference (pointer, file descriptor, unguarded capability, mutable copy) the check can be bypassed, so it must return guarded views or references it can still revoke — which constrains the object's public surface.
Centralised decisions add a dependency in distributed systems: a decision service needs latency and availability budgets, and any decision cache must carry revocation semantics for every replica.
Testability improves only if bypass attempts are exercised: unit tests of the mediator prove that the check works, not that it is complete — path enumeration is the expensive part.

Of Saltzer and Schroeder's eight design principles, complete mediation is historically the least adopted in production systems due to its perceived performance cost, making it a recurring source of bypass vulnerabilities (Smith 2012).

participants.responsibility: The active entity requesting access (user, service, process, thread); it is identified by whatever credential, principal or capability the enforcement layer can verify.

The single decision point that every access attempt passes: it resolves the subject, asks the authority source, and permits or denies the operation. Always invoked, tamperproof with respect to the mediated operations, and small enough to review. Corresponds to NIST SP 800-207's Policy Enforcement Point (PEP).
The resource being accessed; it is reachable only through the mediator, never through references handed directly to callers.

Where the rule lives — an access control list, a capability table, a policy decision point (PDP), a permission model or a kernel rule set; complete mediation requires it to reflect revocations immediately. Corresponds to NIST SP 800-207's Policy Decision Point (PDP).
Records every decision, including denials, at the mediator; it is what turns 'we check everywhere' into evidence that can be examined.

use_cases: Kernels and sandboxes: a seccomp-BPF allow-list and a Landlock ruleset mediate syscalls and file hierarchies so a compromised process cannot reach outside the set it was granted.

Web and API services: authorization middleware re-evaluates a policy on every request instead of trusting the session established at login, and resource-based checks run at the point of use for per-object access.
Data access layers: row-level security or a policy-enforcing gateway checks each query result against the caller's tenant and permissions rather than relying on the privileges of the connection.

Capability systems and membranes: every operation on a wrapped object — including objects returned from earlier calls and callbacks — is intercepted, so restrictions cannot be escaped by taking a reference.
Multi-tenant and administrative surfaces: the same mediator serves interactive, batch and admin callers, each with its own principal, so 'internal' callers get no exemption.
Embedded and device control: a supervisory layer checks every actuation command against the device policy, independent of which subsystem issued it.

Kubernetes admission control: every API server request passes through a chain of validating admission webhooks (OPA Gatekeeper, custom controllers) that re-evaluate policy against the submitted object and current state before the resource is stored; the API server's own enforcement is the final PEP.

Service mesh authorization: Istio or Linkerd proxies enforce mTLS and authorization policies at every mesh connection; for complex policy, Envoy's ext_authz filter forwards decisions to OPA or a custom PDP, closing the gap between L4 connectivity and L7 authorization.

OAuth2/OIDC token revocation: every API request to a protected resource triggers token introspection or a live validation call against the authorization server; cached tokens are treated as leases with short TTL, and revocation events push invalidation to all PEPs via token denylists or OPA push updates.

POSIX filesystem operations with openat2(): Linux 5.6+ RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS and RESOLVE_BENEATH flags make path resolution and access check atomic within a single syscall, eliminating the TOCTOU window between a separate faccessat() and open() pair.

Database row-level security (RLS): PostgreSQL, Oracle VPD, and SQL Server RLS enforce access control inside the database engine so that every query result is filtered against the caller's security context regardless of which application issued it.

Multi-tenant SaaS with per-tenant PEPs: each tenant's requests pass through a tenant-specific authorization policy evaluated by OPA or Cedar, ensuring that a tenant's revoked users lose access on the next call even if a prior call established a long-lived session token.

FreeBSD Capsicum: cap_enter() puts a process into capability mode, after which every operation is mediated by rights bound to the descriptors it already holds — global namespaces (filesystem paths, IPC, network creation) are unavailable, the syscalls permitted in capability mode are a curated, audited list (capabilities.conf), and cap_rights_limit() narrows a descriptor's rights for all later uses, so no ambient authority survives to bypass the check.

AWS IAM: every API call is authorized fresh — the service builds a request context and evaluates it against identity-based policies, resource-based policies, permissions boundaries, Organizations SCPs/RCPs and session policies; the default is implicit deny and an explicit deny anywhere overrides every allow, so no earlier grant is inherited without re-evaluation.

Spring Security: the AuthorizationFilter sits last in the servlet filter chain and evaluates the first matching authorization rule on every request dispatch — REQUEST, FORWARD, INCLUDE and ERROR — so a forwarded or error-dispatched request cannot reach a controller on a decision made for the original request.
avoid_when: The object is accessed exactly once at start-up and the reference is then held privately: check once and keep the reference unreachable, instead of paying for mediation that has nothing left to mediate.

The operation is a tight inner loop over data that has already been confined and can no longer change owner: check at the boundary and hand the loop an immutable view (economy of mechanism) rather than a check per iteration.
The platform already mediates the resource completely (kernel LSM, database row security, managed identity gateway, container runtime): configure it, do not rebuild it in application code.
The component has exactly one entry point and one caller and its whole purpose is the privileged operation (a crypto primitive): least privilege plus a narrow interface is the simpler answer.

No identity or revocation channel can be supplied for a path: a check that has nothing to decide on is worse than no check, because it documents security that is not there — fix the identity model first.
anti_patterns: Check-once-then-trust: authority established at login or connection setup and never re-evaluated, so a revoked subject keeps working until the session ends.
Remembering decisions without a revocation story: authorization results cached in a session, a thread local or an LRU and left stale when policy or entitlements change.
Advisory-only mediation: checks in application code while another path — admin CLI, direct database access, a raw socket, an internal endpoint — reaches the same resource.
Check-then-use with a window: access() then open(), stat() then read, policy check then handle lookup.
A mediator with exemptions: 'system', 'internal' or debug callers skip the check, or the enforcement point can be reconfigured off at runtime.
Trusting the calling layer: assuming that because API gateway or ingress validated the token, downstream services need not re-evaluate it for their own access decisions.
Capability leakage: returning a raw handle, pointer, file descriptor or capability that lets the caller reach the object without returning through the mediator on subsequent accesses.
design_principles: Complete mediation: every access to every object must be checked for authority, which forces a system-wide view that includes initialization, recovery, shutdown and maintenance.
Least privilege: per-access decisions let a subject hold only the rights each operation needs, and let those rights shrink as the operation proceeds.
Economy of mechanism: the decision point must stay small and simple, because it is the component an attacker studies first.
Fail-safe defaults: if the mediator cannot decide (missing identity, unreachable policy, internal error), the access is denied.
Defence in depth: independent enforcement points may each be complete for their layer, so bypassing one does not expose the resource.
Separation of policy and enforcement: the mediator enforces decisions made by a replaceable policy source; the two must not be co-mingled.
best_practices: Check at the point of use: perform the decision in the same operation that touches the resource, not before it.
Interpose as low as feasible (kernel filter, framework middleware, a single facade) so bypassing requires breaking the platform rather than finding a code path.
Keep the mediator small, testable and audited: one decision per access, denials logged, policy in a separate replaceable source.
Treat cached decisions as leases: bound their lifetime, invalidate on revocation and entitlement changes, and never cache across a privilege change.
Enumerate and test the access paths, including batch, recovery, admin and error paths; a mediator is complete by proof, not by intent.
Return guarded views instead of raw references, revoke handles when entitlements change, and remember that resources opened before an enforcement layer starts are outside its guarantees.
For filesystem access, prefer openat2() with RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS or RESOLVE_BENEATH over faccessat() + open() pairs; use O_EXCL for atomic existence-check-and-create.
Implement authorization as a NIST SP 800-207 PDP/PEP pair: every PEP call to the PDP is a fresh decision; OPA, Cedar or AWS IAM Authorizer are canonical implementations.
In multi-layer services (API gateway → service → database), apply mediation at every layer independently; do not assume an upstream check means the downstream call is authorized.
Use CWE-638 mitigations as a checklist: invalidate cached credentials on any identity or permission change; avoid long-lived authorization caches; enumerate all code paths to sensitive resources.
For distributed systems, push revocation events to all PEPs via a token denylist or OPA push updates; polling the PDP on every request is the safest baseline when push is unavailable.
Validate revocation stories in code review: every cached authorization decision needs a corresponding invalidation path triggered by the same event that changes the underlying authority.
sources: Saltzer & Schroeder, "The Protection of Information in Computer Systems", Proceedings of the IEEE 63(9), 1975 — design principle (c): 'Every access to every object must be checked for authority'; the same text warns that proposals to gain performance by remembering the result of an authority check must be examined skeptically, and that remembered results must be systematically updated when authority changes.
https://web.mit.edu/Saltzer/www/publications/protection/Basic.html

Schumacher, Fernandez-Buglioni, Hybertson, Buschmann & Sommerlad, Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering, Wiley 2006 — the security-patterns canon this catalog row belongs to.
https://devguide.owasp.org/en/02-foundations/03-security-principles

MITRE CWE-638 — Not Using Complete Mediation: software that fails to verify access permissions every time a resource is accessed, creating a window for privilege escalation when rights change. https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/638.html

MITRE CWE-367 — Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition: the product checks the state of a resource before using it, but the state can change between check and use. https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/367.html

Wei, Mao, Shen & Venkatakrishnan, "TOCTTOU Vulnerabilities in UNIX-Style File Systems: An Anatomical Study", FAST '05 — systematic enumeration of 224 TOCTOU-prone syscall pairs in Linux VFS and confirmed exploits in rpm, vi, emacs; quantifies exploit success rates from milliseconds (85% for rpm) to unlikely (gedit). https://static.usenix.org/event/fast05/tech/full_papers/wei/wei.pdf

Smith, "A Contemporary Look at Saltzer and Schroeder's 1975 Design Principles", IEEE Security & Privacy 2012 — notes that of Saltzer's eight principles, complete mediation has been 'least adopted' in practice due to performance cost, yet remains the primary underpinning of any protection system.

Heckman & Schell, "Using Proven Reference Monitor Patterns for Security Evaluation", ISSTA 2016 / Sustainability 2016 — maps the three reference monitor properties (completeness/non-bypassability, tamperproof/isolation, verifiability) to modern TCSEC/TNI patterns and shows how their systematic application would have prevented Stuxnet.

NIST SP 800-207 — Zero Trust Architecture: formalizes PDP/PEP model where 'no request is trusted by default based on network location' and every access decision is made per-session against the PDP. https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-207/final

NIST SP 800-207A — Zero Trust Architecture Model for Access Control in Cloud-Native Applications in Multi-Cloud Environments: extends SP 800-207 to service-to-service calls across AWS, Azure and GCP boundaries, requiring a policy enforcement layer above each provider's native IAM.

Priebe, Fernández, Mehlau & Pernul, "A Pattern System for Access Control", IFIP SEC 2006 — formalizes Authorization, RBAC, and MBAC (Attribute-based) patterns as a unified pattern system; complete mediation underpins all three.

Designing Secure Software / Strong Enforcement Patterns, Chapter 4 — Complete Mediation: 'protect all access paths enforcing the same access without exception; wherever possible have a single point where a particular security decision occurs (a guard or bottleneck).' https://designingsecuresoftware.com/text/ch4-enforce-patterns/

Plexicus — CWE-638 Not Using Complete Mediation — practical guidance including architecture/design mitigations: invalidate cached privileges on change, perform complete auth checks before caching, use a single interface for all access checks. https://www.plexicus.ai/cwe/cwe-638-not-using-complete-mediation/

Archman Dev — Complete Mediation and Fail Securely (security-architecture principles guide) — code-level examples of caching with short TTL, circuit-breaker for auth service failure, and fail-closed timeout handling. https://github.com/archman-dev/website/blob/main/docs/security-architecture/principles-and-models/complete-mediation-fail-securely.mdx

AWS Prescriptive Guidance — Using OPA for SaaS Multitenant API Access Control — PDP/PEP architecture for multi-tenant SaaS; centralized PDP with OPA sidecar on each service; covers centralized and distributed PDP models with latency trade-offs. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/saas-multitenant-api-access-authorization/using-opa.html

AWS Blog — Achieving Zero Trust Security on Amazon EKS with Istio — OPA Envoy external authorizer as sidecar PEP; evaluates Rego policies on every request; shows AuthorizationPolicy with CUSTOM action forwarding to OPA. https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/opensource/achieving-zero-trust-security-on-amazon-eks-with-istio/

Cerbos — Policy-Based Access Control (PBAC) — PDP/PEP separation with policy-as-code (YAML + CEL); stateless PDP that evaluates per request; PAP stores policies in Git; audit log of every decision. https://www.cerbos.dev/features-benefits-and-use-cases/pbac.md

OpenID AuthZen — Authorization Design Patterns — PEP/PDP, Provisioning, External API (Resource-Enforcer), Microservices, Authorization Mesh patterns for implementing authorization at scale. https://github.com/openid/authzen/blob/main/patterns/AuthorizationDesignPatterns.md

SentinelOne Vulnerability Database — CVE-2026-22723 (Cloud Foundry UAA Auth Bypass): token revocation logic error lets revoked tokens remain valid; complete mediation failure at token validation boundary. https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-22723/

SentinelOne Vulnerability Database — CVE-2026-59818 (etcd gRPC CRL Bypass): when etcd splits HTTP and gRPC onto separate listeners, CRL enforcement was applied only to the HTTP listener; gRPC connections bypassed revocation check entirely. https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-59818/

Armis / CVE-2014-2237 — OpenStack Keystone Memcache Trust Token Bypass: trustee token not added to token-index-list, preventing bulk revocation; revocation events not propagated to memcache backend. https://cve.armis.com/CVE-2014-2237

SentinelOne Vulnerability Database — CVE-2026-42508 (Go Crypto Auth Bypass): golang.org/x/crypto only checked top-level key for @revoked marker, not key.SignatureKey subfield; a revoked CA signing subkey was silently trusted. https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-42508/

System Shardening — TOCTOU Vulnerability Defences: Eliminating Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use Races Across the Stack — comprehensive defense taxonomy: openat2() RESOLVE flags, O_EXCL, double-fetch prevention in kernel code, database SELECT FOR UPDATE, idempotency keys. https://www.systemshardening.com/articles/cross-cutting/toctou-vulnerability-defences/

Safeguard.sh — Multi-Cloud Security: Identity, Segmentation, Policy — federating identity across AWS/Azure/GCP with OPA as unified policy engine; service mesh mTLS as application-layer enforcement; references NIST SP 800-207A for multi-cloud TOCTOU. https://safeguard.sh/resources/blog/multi-cloud-security-architecture-fundamentals

FreeBSD manual page capsicum — capability mode restricts a process to operations on descriptors it holds and rights bound to them; the system calls allowed in capability mode are a curated, audited kernel list (capabilities.conf). https://man.freebsd.org/cgi/man.cgi?capsicum=

Watson, Anderson, Laurie & Kennaway, "Capsicum: Practical Capabilities for UNIX", USENIX Security 2010 — every operation in capability mode is mediated by a per-descriptor rights mask and ambient authority to global namespaces is removed, the kernel form of checking every access. https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/sec10/tech/full_papers/Watson.pdf

AWS IAM — How AWS enforcement code logic evaluates requests to allow or deny access: every API call is evaluated against a freshly built request context with implicit deny by default and explicit deny overriding allow across all applicable policy types. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic_policy-eval-denyallow.html

Spring Security — Authorize HttpServletRequests: AuthorizationFilter evaluates authorization for every request dispatch (REQUEST, FORWARD, INCLUDE, ERROR) and is placed last in the default filter chain. https://docs.spring.io/spring-security/reference/servlet/authorization/authorize-http-requests.html

OWASP Annotated ASVS 2.1 — Principle of complete mediation: every page requires authentication by default unless explicitly public; a single overly broad whitelist entry (e.g. a framework anonymous rule) breaks mediation — audit guidance for finding exactly this failure. https://owasp-aasvs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/requirement-2.1.html
